question: Copper forming chelates with peptide linkages under alkaline conditions turns a solution violet, which is the _____ and the standard way to show protein is present.
questions: Because it reports the peptide bond rather than any particular molecule, the _____ answers to anything carrying enough of them, which is a limit as well as a convenience.
Clinical laboratories measure serum total protein with the _____, though a refractometer is quicker and cheaper and agrees with it closely enough to substitute.
abstract:
Cells are built from four classes of molecule, carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids and proteins, and the oldest way of asking which of them is in a sample is a reagent that changes colour when it is. The biuret test is the one for protein: at alkaline pH copper forms chelates with the peptide linkages of a protein, and the solution turns violet. What it reports is therefore the peptide bond rather than any particular protein, so anything carrying enough of them will answer. It is no classroom relic, and the biuret method is used routinely in reference and in-clinic laboratories to measure serum total protein. Nor is it irreplaceable, and a refractometer, quicker and cheaper, correlates strongly enough with it to be used instead in cattle and goats.

Sugars have their own colour reactions, and reducing sugars have been determined by the Somogyi-Nelson, phenol-sulfuric, anthrone, Fehling and dinitrosalicylic acid methods. Some of the older ones are laborious, Fehling's involving precipitation and titration, and newer routes are designed to report not only that the sugar is there but how much of it is. That is the direction of travel: a colour change answers whether, and a calibrated assay answers how much. The descendant of these tests that a reader is most likely to meet is the urine dipstick, whose reagent pads report protein, glucose, blood and several other things by colour, each read against a printed chart. Every pad has its documented false positives and negatives, the protein pad reading positive in alkaline or concentrated urine and negative when the protein present is not albumin, and reference ranges themselves shift with the substrates and reagents an assay uses.
